title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether adding a deterministic network verifier to a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Using N = 240 paired intents (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across paired arms), the run completed as planned (planned episodes = 480, completed = 480, model calls used = 240). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline = 240/240 = 1.0, guarded = 240/240 = 1.0; paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. No validator‑triggered repairs were applied because every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator. Importantly, under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast can only differ if the shared initial candidate fails validation or if a validator‑triggered repair is applied; we explicitly report this constraint in Abstract and Conclusion. We provide the preregistered design, exact execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, and a failure‑analytic interpretation of the null paired outcome together with artifact‑based recommendations for future emulation‑grounded NetOps evaluations.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into concrete device configurations and to automate NetOps workflows. Execution‑grounded evaluations that place LLM agents into emulated networks reveal planning and workflow failures that token‑level metrics miss [1]. A practical mitigation pattern is generate–validate–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration, run a deterministic validator that checks intent and workflow invariants, and invoke repair when violations are detected [2,3]. We preregistered and ran a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment to quantify whether adding a deterministic verifier (with at most one validator‑triggered repair) reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline when the same initial LLM candidate is shared across paired arms. Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered paired confirmatory run and complete execution accounting (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) artifact‑grounded reporting of exact per‑call traces and analysis artifacts; and (3) a failure‑analytic interpretation of a null paired outcome with concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for future experimental designs.
sections.related_work: Emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks and closed‑loop agent evaluations show that multi‑step planning and execution faults arise in task‑oriented NetOps agents and motivate executable testing frameworks [1]. Prior systems and program‑repair work have formalized generate–validate and generate–validate–repair architectures and demonstrated reductions of syntactic and some semantic failures when validator coverage and repair search are adequate [2,4]. Survey and position pieces argue for tool augmentation (verifiers, knowledge graphs), uncertainty calibration, and layered defenses for agentic systems, while noting unresolved empirical questions about verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts [3,5]. We use these sources to motivate (a) an emulation‑grounded paired design, (b) a deterministic validator as the guarding mechanism, and (c) adversarial and distribution‑shift task subsets to probe robustness.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the full design (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate). For clarity in this manuscript and in archived analysis artifacts, unsafe_apply = 1 and safe_apply = 0; many archived fields label safe outcomes as "success" (safe_apply = 1 in archived "success" fields), and we explicitly map those terms here: archived baseline_success_count = 240 corresponds to baseline safe_apply = 240 (i.e., baseline unsafe_apply = 0). Design and sampling: N = 240 distinct tasks executed as paired episodes (baseline LLM‑only vs guarded GVR) with task composition: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial 20% (48). Generation semantics and adapter contract: the registered adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused for both arms; the guarded arm could invoke at most one validator‑triggered repair per task. This semantics was preregistered and constrains the estimand interpretation: the guarded arm can only change paired outcomes if the shared initial candidate fails the deterministic validator or a repair is applied. Models and runtime: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" (execution/model_configuration.json). The model adapter emitted one shared initial generation per pair (hosted_model_call_event_count = 240; model_calls_used = 240). Validator and repair budget: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 was used for validation; repair budget per guarded task was at most one repair call. Stopping rules and missingness: planned_episode_count = 480 (240 pairs × 2), maximum_model_calls = 480, preregistered retry policy allowed up to two infra‑recovery attempts; primary analysis treatment excluded unrecoverable infra failures (none occurred). Scoring and analysis: each episode was executed in the emulator and deterministically scored safe (0) or unsafe (1) by the validator and emulator oracle. The registered analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency table, 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Mapping estimand to artifacts: primary outcome and contingency are archived as analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; per‑condition summaries are in analysis/condition_summary.csv; the analysis log records bootstrap parameters in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.
sections.results: Execution accounting: the adapter completed the run as registered: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240; hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 (shared initial generation), model_calls_used = 240 (execution_manifest.record). Primary binary outcomes: baseline safe_apply count = 240/240 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0), guarded safe_apply count = 240/240 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). Paired contingency: n11 = 240 (both safe), n10 = 0 (guarded unsafe & baseline safe), n01 = 0 (baseline unsafe & guarded safe), n00 = 0 (both unsafe) as recorded in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv. Inference: the paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] using 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Repair and validator activity: no validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode (repair_attempts = 0 across analysis/repair logs); consequently every guarded final configuration equaled the shared initial candidate and matched the baseline final configuration. Missingness and flags: analysis/missingness_summary.csv and analysis/contamination_summary.csv report zero infra failures and zero 'possible false‑safe' flags; therefore no preregistered exclusions affected the primary analysis. Representative examples: selected per‑task validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000004-guarded.json) show detailed validation metadata (difficulty levels, required_command_count) and validator PASS semantics; these artifacts substantiate that validator checks were exercised and passed rather than being skipped.
sections.discussion: Null paired outcome interpretation: the preregistered H1 (GVR reduces unsafe‑apply rate compared to LLM‑only) is not supported by these data. This null is informative and arises from two artifact‑grounded facts: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one shared LLM output per task that was reused across arms, and (2) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 passed every shared initial candidate, so the guarded pipeline had no occasion to apply repairs or alter any paired outcome. Under these conditions the paired contrast is degenerate (no discordant pairs). Statistical interpretation: when n10 = n01 = 0 the McNemar statistic is degenerate and the bootstrap CI collapses to zero width; the analysis executor's outputs (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, seed = 1729) correctly reflect the observed data and do not indicate an analysis error. Design implications and recommendations (artifact‑grounded): (A) To measure verifier/repair benefit in a paired framework, relax shared_initial_candidate semantics to permit independent initial generations per arm or increase generator variability (for example, allow independent sampling seeds or higher generation budget for one arm) so validators have opportunities to detect candidate failures. (B) Increase repair search budget and allow multi‑iteration repair strategies; here the repair budget (≤1) and validator coverage combined to preclude repairs. (C) Strengthen adversary sampling beyond a single preregistered attacker seed when evaluating prompt‑injection defenses; our adversarial set was generated under a fixed attacker seed as declared in the preregistration. (D) Broaden deterministic verifier semantic coverage and instrument routine cross‑checks between verifier PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases; the preregistration planned such cross‑checks (deterministic reconciliation artifacts are archived). Threats to validity: internal validity is constrained by the shared_initial_candidate semantics and single‑model execution (gpt‑5‑mini); construct validity is limited by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage; external validity is limited by the emulation corpus (NetConfArena‑style synthetic tasks) and single‑provider model scope; conclusion validity is constrained because baseline unsafe rate = 0 rendered the paired contrast untestable in this run. All these threats and recommendations are tied to archived artifacts and execution logs.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based configuration generation. Every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation confirms that no validator‑triggered repairs occurred because the single shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator in every task. Critically, under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm can only affect paired outcomes when initial candidates fail validation or when repairs are applied; we state this constraint explicitly to avoid implying that the paired contrast measured an independent effect of constrained prompting or prompt engineering. We archive the preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable follow‑up experiments that vary generation semantics, adversary strength, or verifier coverage. Future paired studies should permit generator variability between arms or increase repair/search budgets to produce informative discordant pairs and thereby measure verifier benefit empirically.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: The experiment used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Runtime sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset); unset temperature does not imply deterministic sampling by the hosted provider and sampling nondeterminism remains possible; all model‑call metadata were archived. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock; a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the lock; no manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred post‑lock. Preregistered generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms), so only validator‑triggered repairs could create paired divergences; this semantics is explicitly used and reported in Methods and Results. Execution accounting (archived): planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240. Immutable master prompt: the initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Reproducibility pointer: archived execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are available in the execution bundle (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/).
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidates failing validation.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed attacker protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
